To concede means to admit or give up something, even when you don't want to. The most important feeling hiding inside this word is reluctance — you're not happily agreeing or freely giving. You're doing it because the situation has forced you to, because the facts are too strong to deny, or because continuing to resist no longer makes sense.

That reluctant, against-your-own-interest quality is what makes "concede" precise and powerful. It's not just admitting or giving up — it's doing so from a position where you wished things were different.

1. Conceding in Thought or Argument — "I admit this is true"

When you concede a point, you acknowledge that something is true or valid, even though it works against your own position or argument.

Imagine you and a friend are arguing. You've been insisting that a certain movie was released in 2005. Your friend shows you proof it was 2007. You say, "Fine, I concede — you're right." You're not changing your whole opinion about the movie. You're simply accepting that on this specific point, you were wrong.

This is the most common everyday use of the word. Notice:

  • You don't have to agree with everything, just the specific thing you're conceding.
  • A good debater sometimes concedes a minor point to strengthen their overall argument — they are saying, "Yes, that small thing is true, but here's why my bigger point still stands."
  • You can say "I concede that..." followed by the thing you are admitting: "I concede that the process was flawed, but the final result was still correct."

2. Conceding in Competition or Conflict — "I give this up to you"

When you concede in a competition, a negotiation, a war, or an election, you are surrendering something — a claim, a victory, a territory, a privilege — to the other side.

A few vivid examples:

  • A politician who concedes an election is publicly announcing that they accept they have lost. They are giving up their claim to the win. This is called conceding defeat.
  • In chess, a player concedes when they tip over their king — they are handing the victory to their opponent rather than playing to the bitter end.
  • In a peace negotiation, a country might concede territory — it gives up land to the other side as part of an agreement.
  • In soccer and other sports, a team concedes a goal when the opposing team scores. The team didn't want to let that goal in — it was forced upon them. This usage is especially common in British English.

Conceding is not the same as freely agreeing or voluntarily giving.
If you happily hand your friend a gift, you didn't concede it to them. But if you've been arguing over who deserves the last slice of pizza, and the evidence piles up against you, and you finally say "Alright, it's yours" — that's a concession.

Conceding is not the same as total surrender.
You can concede one thing while still holding your ground on everything else. A lawyer in a courtroom might concede that the defendant was present at the scene, but still argue the defendant is not guilty. Conceding one point does not mean losing the whole argument.

Conceding can be a sign of strength, not weakness.
Wise negotiators, lawyers, and thinkers often strategically concede minor points. It builds trust, shows intellectual honesty, and lets them focus their energy on the bigger battle. Refusing to ever concede anything — even the obviously true — makes you look unreasonable.

Notice the different grammatical patterns:

  • Concede + that (clause): "She conceded that the plan had some weaknesses." (admitting something is true)
  • Concede + noun: "He conceded defeat gracefully." / "The team conceded three goals." (giving something up or allowing something)
  • Concede + something + to someone: "They conceded the northern regions to the opposing army." (surrendering something to a specific party)
  • Concede to (someone/something): "He eventually conceded to her demands." (yielding to pressure or a request)

Since you'll encounter similar words, here's how they differ:

Admit is broader and more neutral. You admit a fact, a mistake, or a feeling. There's no necessary sense of giving something up to an opponent. "I admit I was nervous" — there's no competition here. Concede carries a stronger sense of a position or claim being given up to someone else.

Acknowledge is even more neutral — it simply means recognizing that something exists or is true, with no reluctance required at all. "She acknowledged the applause."

Yield focuses on giving way — stepping back, letting someone else pass or take precedence. It's physically and metaphorically about making room. Concede is about admitting or surrendering a specific point, right, or victory.

Surrender is more total and dramatic — it usually means giving up completely, often in a conflict. Conceding can be partial. You concede a point or a goal; you surrender everything.

To concede is to admit something is true or to give something up to another person — reluctantly, and usually because the facts, the situation, or the power of the moment has left you no better option.
